Zebra finch · 11-class call type · leave-birds-out

What the call-type space actually looks like

The accuracy table said AVES beats colony-specific pretraining by 0.034. That is one number over a whole task. What follows asks which calls get confused, whether the two encoders fail on the same clips, whether either space is organised by call type at all — and then the question that matters for a species we have no labels for: can any of this be decided without ground truth?

Only 40% of the errors are shared. AVES gets 307 clips right that run11 misses, and run11 gets 193 right that AVES misses. Two encoders that failed the same way would be redundant; these are not, which is the concrete reason an ensemble helps here and why concatenating their features is worth separating from averaging their decisions.

What this does not show

Every number here is the call-type task on curated clips. It says nothing about detection or about transfer to another colony — the BirdPark holdout lives on Savio and was unreachable when this was produced. And Di (18 clips) and LT should not be read as evidence of anything on their own.

Part II · With no decoder anywhere

Everything above used a trained logistic regression. A readout can find a direction that separates classes even when the embedding does not natively group them — so "AVES decodes better" and "AVES's space is better organised" are different claims. Nothing below fits a classifier. Labels are used only to score structure that was discovered without them.

The short answer

AVES, but not unanimously — and the disagreement is the interesting part. Across three decoder-free measures × three spaces, AVES wins 8 of 9. run11's single hold-out is local structure: a clip's nearest neighbours share its call type more often in run11's space, at all twelve layers. AVES wins everything global.

Three things fall out of that table. Ward AMI: AVES ahead at 10 of 12 layers (run11's two wins, L4 and L11, are +0.0007 and +0.0016 — ties). kNN: run11 ahead at 12 of 12, and the gap widens with depth. Silhouette: AVES ahead at 12 of 12, and run11 turns negative from L6 onward — past the middle of the stack, the average clip sits closer to some other call type's centre than to its own.

The probe was reading a different layer than the geometry

Chosen without labels, the best layers are run11 L2 and AVES L0. The supervised probe picked L3 for both. AVES's structure is richest at layer 0 — before a single transformer block. That is consistent with the earlier finding that the CNN front end carries most of the value here, and it is a warning about layer selection: the depth that decodes best is not the depth that is best organised.

Does the algorithm decide it?

Algorithm AMI run11AMI AVES hom run11hom AVES bird run11bird AVES
Ward0.56400.66500.57500.68480.28610.2539
k-means0.48400.61200.50440.63560.26870.2344
HDBSCAN0.50830.64900.36340.49710.13520.1732

No. AVES leads on all three, and by a margin that survives resampling: +0.0912 [+0.0528, +0.1283] on Ward AMI, bootstrapped over birds. Ward beats k-means for both encoders — the clusters are not spherical, so k-means is the wrong tool, which is worth remembering the next time a k is chosen by convenience.

HDBSCAN is the most honest of the three because nobody tells it how many groups to find. Given free rein it found 4 for both encoders and discarded two-thirds of the clips as noise (67% for run11, 74% for AVES). Neither space contains eleven clean density peaks. The call types that survive unsupervised discovery are a handful of acoustically distinct ones — consistent with Part I, where a few classes were near-perfect and the rest bled together.

Does UMAP change the answer?

Space Ward run11Ward AVESgap kNN run11kNN AVESgap
full 768-d0.56400.6650+0.10100.85900.8523-0.0067
UMAP 10-d0.62870.6744+0.04570.86380.8674+0.0035
UMAP 2-d0.62650.6852+0.05870.84390.8425-0.0014

It changes the size of the gap, not the winner. UMAP helps run11 considerably more than it helps AVES — Ward AMI rises 0.564 → 0.629 for run11 but only 0.665 → 0.674 for AVES, cutting the gap from +0.101 to +0.046. Read that as: run11's call-type structure is present but tangled, and a nonlinear reduction untangles some of it, whereas AVES's is already close to linearly accessible.

The kNN reversal is real but tiny. run11 leads by 0.0067 in the native space and by 0.0014 in 2-d; AVES leads by 0.0035 at 10-d. All three are small enough that the honest statement is local neighbourhood quality is roughly a tie, with run11 slightly ahead where it is not reduced.

What this means

Colony-specific pretraining bought local discrimination — run11 places acoustically similar calls from its own colony near each other slightly better. It did not buy global organisation — the large-scale geometry of AVES's space aligns better with call type and is less confounded by bird identity, at nearly every layer, under every clustering algorithm, in every dimensionality. Since clustering is a global operation, the unsupervised verdict matches the supervised one: AVES.

Two caveats on the method

The bootstrap resamples birds against a fixed clustering — it captures the metric's sampling variability, not the variability of refitting Ward, so the true interval is wider than shown. And AMI is used throughout rather than NMI or purity because both of those inflate with k and would hand the win to whichever run happened to use more clusters.

Part III · Clustering as a classifier

AMI says the groups line up with call type, but it is not an accuracy and cannot be put next to the probe's 0.81 / 0.85. So: cluster the training birds with no labels, give each cluster the single majority label of its training members, assign held-out clips to the nearest training centroid, and score. One integer per cluster is the only supervision that enters.

Most of the probe's accuracy is already in the geometry

At its best k a cluster vote reaches 0.7271 for run11 and 0.7714 for AVES — 90% and 91% of what a trained 11-way logistic regression gets, from one label per cluster instead of 768 fitted weights per class. The decoder is mostly reading structure that is already there, not creating it.

The reversal, and why it is not real

Selected by silhouette — genuinely label-free — run11 appears to win: 0.6905 against AVES's 0.5106 under Ward, and 0.6761 against 0.3960 under k-means. That contradicts every other measure on this page, so it is worth looking at why.

Encoder · algorithmsilhouette-kbest k kcost of choosingk chosen per fold
run11 · ward0.69050.726670-0.0360[40, 20, 70, 40, 25]
run11 · kmeans0.67610.727170-0.0510[20, 30, 16, 20, 20]
aves · ward0.51060.757670-0.2471[4, 40, 8, 16, 4]
aves · kmeans0.39600.771455-0.3754[4, 4, 4, 4, 4]

Silhouette picks k=4 for AVES, in four folds out of five under k-means. Four clusters can express at most four of the eleven labels, so the vote is capped near 0.396 no matter how good the space is. The criterion is not measuring the thing we need: silhouette rewards few, well-separated, roughly convex blobs, and AVES's space is more coarsely clumpy — which is exactly why it scored higher on silhouette in Part II. The same property that made it look good there makes the k-chooser fail here.

At matched k, the earlier verdict holds

AVES is ahead at every k from 6 upward, in both algorithms — by +0.086 at k=11, the true class count (0.5583 vs 0.6442). The apparent run11 win is entirely an artefact of how k was chosen, not a property of the representations.

The lesson, which generalises past this page

Accuracy keeps climbing to k=55–70 — five to six times the number of classes. Call types are not single blobs; each needs several clusters to be covered. Any unsupervised protocol that fixes k at the number of classes, or picks it with a compactness criterion, will understate a representation badly — and will understate the better representation more. That is worth remembering wherever a k is chosen, including the k=100 / k=200 pseudo-label decision in pretraining. Part IV pushes k far enough to find out where the climbing stops, and the answer turns out to change what this section means.

Part IV · Doing it for real, where there are no labels

Part III chose k two ways: by silhouette, which was label-free and wrong, and by test accuracy, which was right and unavailable. Neither is what you would do on a bat colony. The fix is not to pretend the oracle away — it is to calibrate the procedure once, here, on the one corpus that has ground truth, and then carry the procedure rather than the answer.

The setup

Five encoders, same architecture, same 768 dimensions, same layer 3 — a genuinely hard ranking problem, since their true accuracies span only 0.052. Seven strictly label-free criteria. A sixth “encoder” that is AVES with every dimension independently shuffled across clips: identical marginals, no joint structure, and the honest floor. Labels are consulted only after every blind choice has been committed.

8 · There is no k to find

Before asking which criterion picks k well, check that the question has an answer. It does not.

EncoderPeak accuracyat k 1-NN ceilingpeak − 1-NN
AVES-base-all0.802816000.7995+0.0032
AVES-base-core0.79544500.7887+0.0067
AVES0.782816000.7843-0.0015
run11 (ZF)0.76936500.7699-0.0006
birdAVES-biox0.76883000.7649+0.0038
shuffled null0.1858300.1243+0.0615

Every real encoder’s curve rises monotonically and lands on its own 1-nearest-neighbour accuracy, to within 0.007. That is not a coincidence, it is the definition: as k approaches the number of training clips, each cluster holds one clip and the majority vote becomes 1-NN. Cluster-then-vote is a compression curve, not a search for the correct number of groups. The oracle-k numbers in Part III were measuring how much compression the geometry tolerates — they were never evidence about a true k.

A free diagnostic, and the one place the curve’s shape does tell you something

The shuffled null is the only curve that peaks and falls back — 0.1858 at k=30, down to 0.1243 at 1-NN, against a majority floor of 0.1797. A rising-to-ceiling curve means there is structure; an interior bump that collapses means the bump was majority-vote overfitting. You can draw this plot on any corpus, labelled or not, as long as you have some readout to score — and on an unlabelled corpus the shuffled null gives you the comparison for free.

9 · Which criterion ranks representations correctly?

k is not selectable. But choosing between encoders at a matched k is a real question with a real answer, and it is the question you actually face.

Criterionmean ρ over 12 kρ > 0 at
bird-held-out stability+0.4110 / 12
bootstrap stability+0.379 / 12
gap statistic+0.035 / 12
prediction strength−0.183 / 12
Davies–Bouldin−0.301 / 12
silhouette−0.501 / 12
Calinski–Harabasz−0.661 / 12
AMI — uses the labels +0.7312 / 12

The split is clean and it runs along one seam. Reproducibility criteria — would I find these same groups again in birds I have not seen? — track the truth. Compactness criteria — are these blobs tight and round? — do not merely fail; they rank the encoders backwards, positive at one value of k out of twelve each.

Why compactness inverts, and why you should have expected it

It is the same mechanism that produced the fake reversal in Part III. Silhouette, Calinski–Harabasz and Davies–Bouldin all reward few, tight, convex clumps. The better encoder here spreads a call type across several sub-groups rather than one ball — which is exactly what lets it reach a higher accuracy at large k, and exactly what these criteria penalise. The property that makes a representation good is the property they score down.

How much weight this can carry

Five encoders. Their true accuracies span 0.052. At n=5 a single ρ of ±0.3 is noise and even ρ=+0.9 is one swap from non-significance, so the claim rests on the sign holding across k — 10 of 12 and 9 of 12 — not on any one correlation. All five share an architecture, a dimensionality and a layer, so this is ranking within a family, not across model classes.

What it would have told us blind: over k = 13 to 140, bird-held-out stability places run11 in the bottom two of the five at 8 of those 10 values of k, with a median rank of worst. The labelled evaluation puts it bottom-two at 10 of 10. A procedure that never sees a call-type label reaches the same verdict on colony-specific pretraining that the whole supervised pipeline reaches.

10 · Can the criterion tell there is anything there at all?

On a new species this is the first question, not the last: is this structure, or is it the clustering algorithm doing what clustering algorithms always do?

Almost everything passes this easier test, and the stability measures pass it by two and a half orders of magnitude — the null scores 0.0014 where the real encoders score 0.489. The exception is the gap statistic, which reads 1.91 on a real embedding and 1.45 on destroyed noise. It cannot distinguish the two, which retires it here — and explains why it scored an apparently perfect zero cost when it simply named the largest k on offer every time.

11 · The protocol, for a corpus with no ground truth

This is a sequence, and the order matters: each step is only valid once the one above it has passed.

StepDo thisBecause
1Shuffle your own feature columns and run everything twice. It is the only floor you get for free, and it is what makes every number below interpretable.
2Plot the readout against k on a log axis, out to the 1-NN limit. Rising-to-ceiling means structure. Peak-then-fall means you are fitting the majority vote.
3Fix k from your budget — codebook size, how many units you can afford to listen to — and report a curve, never a single k. There is no natural k to discover. Any criterion claiming to find one is answering a degenerate question.
4Rank representations by held-out-individual stability at matched k, in the band k ≈ 13–140. The only family that tracked the truth here. Below that band it inverts; above k≈200 the encoders converge and there is nothing left to rank.
5Do not use silhouette, Calinski–Harabasz, Davies–Bouldin or the gap statistic to choose between representations. The first three rank them backwards. The fourth cannot tell a real embedding from shuffled noise.
What this does and does not license

It licenses running the protocol on bat or chick recordings and believing the ranking it gives you, because the ranking survived the one calibration available. It does not license believing any particular k, and it does not license a claim about how many call types a species has. Stability’s own argmax lands at k = 4–25 across these encoders, below the 11 human call types and in line with the k=4 that HDBSCAN found independently in Part II — but ARI declines with k for generic combinatorial reasons, so that peak is biased toward coarseness by construction. It is a hint about super-groups, not a repertoire count.

Part IV asks whether any of this can be decided blind: seven label-free criteria across 12 values of k for five same-architecture encoders plus a column-shuffled null, from zfeval/experiments/calltype_blindselect.py, with the k grid pushed to 1600 and the exact 1-NN limit added by calltype_kceiling.py (paper/figures/calltype/calltype_blindselect.json, calltype_kceiling.json, blindselect_report.txt). Written up as knowledge finding 050.

Part II adds a decoder-free comparison: Ward / k-means / HDBSCAN, leave-one-out kNN and silhouette, each recomputed in the full 768-d space and after UMAP to 10-d and 2-d, from zfeval/experiments/calltype_unsup.py (paper/figures/calltype/calltype_unsup.json).

Cohort: 3,412 clips, 48 birds, 11 classes, leave-birds-out StratifiedGroupKFold(5). Probe: standardise → multinomial logistic regression, mean-pooled embeddings, each clip encoded at its own length.
